passage_text: A student heats about 2 g of lead nitrate powder in a dry boiling tube over a flame. After a short time, brown fumes are seen and a yellow solid remains in the tube.
A student heats green crystals of ferrous sulphate in a dry boiling tube. The green colour changes, and a smell like burning sulphur is noticed.
A student adds sodium sulphate solution to barium chloride solution in a beaker. A white substance separates out immediately.
A student heats copper powder in a china dish and a black coating forms on the copper. Hydrogen gas is then passed over the hot, black-coated copper, and the surface turns brown again.

Three test tubes are set up with clean iron nails. Tube A: tap water, open to air. Tube B: boiled distilled water with a layer of oil on top. Tube C: anhydrous calcium chloride, tightly stoppered. After one week the nails are examined.

Anil left an opened packet of potato chips and a bottle of cooking oil in the kitchen for several weeks. Both developed an unpleasant smell and taste. A sealed packet of the same chips kept beside them stayed fresh.

A student mixes about 20 g of solid barium hydroxide with about 10 g of ammonium chloride in a beaker placed on a wet wooden plank and stirs with a glass rod. After a short time, the beaker feels very cold and sticks to the plank. A smell of ammonia is noticed.
